question: Why do you want to become a social worker?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific motivation grounded in real exposure to the field, not just a general wish to help people.

bullets: Point to a specific experience or realisation that pulled you toward the profession
Show you understand social work as skilled, structured practice, not just kindness
Connect the motivation to what you want to spend a career doing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started volunteering at a youth centre in my town two years ago, and what struck me wasn't just that the kids needed help, it was watching the staff social worker actually change a family's situation by knowing which services to connect them with and how to advocate for them. That showed me social work isn't just being caring, it's a real skill set of assessment and advocacy. I want to build that skill set myself, because I've seen how much difference it makes when someone has it and how much gets missed when nobody does.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I want to help people' with nothing more specific
Describing social work as just being kind or a good listener
No concrete experience or story backing the claim
followUps: What part of that experience surprised you most?

question: Why do you want to study social work at this university specifically?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure and placements, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific module, placement partner, or teaching approach
Explain why that feature matters to the kind of social worker you want to become
Show awareness of what makes this course distinct from others
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your placement structure and noticed you place first-years in community settings before statutory ones, which appealed to me because I want to understand a community's own resources before I learn the more formal casework side. I also read about your mental health module being co-taught with people who have lived experience, which matches how I think this training should work, learning with people rather than just about them. That combination is why this course specifically, not just any social work degree.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would fit any social work programme
Citing rankings instead of course content
Not knowing the difference between statutory and voluntary sector placements
followUps: What are you hoping to learn from your first placement?

question: What experience do you have that's relevant to social work, and what did you learn from it?
lookingFor: Concrete, reflected-on experience with vulnerable people, showing real learning rather than a résumé line.

bullets: Describe a specific placement, volunteering role, or caring responsibility
Explain what you actually did, not just the title of the role
Reflect on a moment that taught you something about the work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've spent the last year volunteering at a food bank that also runs a welfare advice desk, mostly helping people fill out benefits forms and just sitting with them while they waited. One afternoon a man broke down because he was ashamed to be there, and I realised the practical help mattered less in that moment than just not making him feel judged. It taught me that dignity is as much a part of the work as the paperwork, and that's stayed with me.

commonMistakes: Listing experience with no reflection on what it taught them
Describing the setting but not their actual role in it
Overstating responsibilities they didn't really have
followUps: How did that experience change how you think about the job?

question: Have you read anything recently, book, article, or report, that shaped how you think about social work?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine engagement with the field beyond the school curriculum, with the ability to discuss it critically.

bullets: Name a specific, credible source, not just 'I read about it online'
Summarise the core idea accurately and briefly
Say what it changed in your thinking or what you'd question about it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read a serious case review into a child protection failure, and what struck me wasn't the individual mistakes but how many professionals had a piece of the picture and none of them had the whole thing. It made me think differently about interagency communication, that it's not a soft skill on top of the job, it's often the difference between a child being protected or not. It's made me want to understand information-sharing systems properly rather than assuming good intentions are enough.

commonMistakes: Naming something vague with no real detail
Summarising without any personal reaction or critique
Picking a source with no real connection to social work practice
followUps: What would you have done differently if you were one of the professionals involved?

subtopic: Social work vs psychology or counselling
question: How is social work different from psychology or counselling, and why did you choose this over those?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate understanding of what distinguishes social work, especially its focus on the person's environment and practical circumstances.

bullets: Explain that social work looks at the person in their environment, not just their internal world
Mention social work's practical and advocacy role, like housing, benefits, safeguarding
Give a personal reason this suits you rather than dismissing the other fields
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Counselling tends to focus on someone's internal world, working through their thoughts and feelings in a fairly contained setting, whereas social work looks at the whole picture around a person, their housing, their finances, their family, and often has to act on that picture, not just talk about it. I respect counselling, but I'm drawn to the practical, sometimes urgent side of the job, actually changing someone's circumstances, not only their outlook. That mix of relationship and action is what pulled me toward social work specifically.

commonMistakes: Saying the fields are basically the same
Putting down psychology or counselling as less serious
Giving no personal reason for the choice
followUps: Do you think social workers need any counselling skills too?

question: What do you think are the core values that should guide a social worker's practice?
lookingFor: Knowledge of the profession's actual value base, like dignity, self-determination, and social justice, put in the applicant's own words.

bullets: Name values like respecting dignity, self-determination, and confidentiality
Include social justice, not just individual care
Give a brief example of what a value looks like in practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For me the core ones are respecting people's dignity and their right to make their own decisions, even when I might not agree with those decisions, and holding confidentiality carefully because trust is the whole foundation of the relationship. I'd also add social justice, because social work isn't just fixing individual problems, it's noticing when the same problem keeps showing up because of an unfair system and pushing back on that too. Self-determination is the one I think about most, because it means genuinely listening rather than deciding what's best for someone.

commonMistakes: Listing values with no real understanding of what they mean in practice
Only focusing on individual care and ignoring social justice
Confusing self-determination with just letting people do anything
followUps: What happens when self-determination conflicts with someone's safety?

question: A client tells you something in confidence that suggests a child in their household may be at risk. What do you do?
lookingFor: Understanding that confidentiality in social work is not absolute, and that safeguarding takes priority, handled with sensitivity.

bullets: State clearly that confidentiality has limits when safety is involved
Explain you'd follow safeguarding procedures, not just personal judgement
Show you'd try to be honest with the client about that limit where possible
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand confidentiality is central to trust, but it isn't absolute, if there's a real risk to a child, I have a duty to act on that even if it damages the relationship with the client. I'd follow my agency's safeguarding procedure and raise it with my supervisor rather than deciding alone, because that kind of judgement shouldn't rest on one person's read of a conversation. Where I could, I'd try to be upfront with the client from the start that this is one of the limits of confidentiality, so it isn't a shock if I do have to act.

commonMistakes: Saying they would keep the confidence no matter what
Deciding to act entirely alone without involving a supervisor or process
Not mentioning being transparent with clients about confidentiality limits
followUps: How would you explain that decision to the client afterward?

question: A client asks you to bend a rule slightly because you believe it would genuinely help them. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that balances compassion for the individual with fairness to others and professional accountability.

bullets: Acknowledge the pull of wanting to help, without pretending it's simple
Explain why consistent, transparent rules matter, even when they feel unfair in one case
Show they'd raise it through proper channels rather than act unilaterally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd feel the pull to just help them, but I'd remind myself that rules exist partly to make sure everyone gets treated fairly, not only the people who ask persuasively. So I wouldn't bend it quietly, but I also wouldn't just refuse and move on, I'd raise it with my supervisor and ask whether there's a legitimate exception process or whether the policy itself needs questioning. If it turned out the rule really was unfair in general, that's useful information for changing it properly rather than working around it case by case.

commonMistakes: Agreeing to bend the rule without escalating it anywhere
Refusing outright with no empathy for the client's situation
Treating the rule as beyond question even when it might be genuinely unfair
followUps: What if your supervisor disagreed with you?

question: What do you understand by a strengths-based approach in social work, and why does it matter?
lookingFor: Understanding that strengths-based practice builds on a person's existing resources and resilience rather than only cataloguing problems.

bullets: Explain the shift from a deficit view of the person to identifying their existing capacities
Give a concrete example of what this looks like in practice
Note the risk of it being used to excuse under-resourcing real needs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A strengths-based approach means starting from what a person already has, their skills, relationships, and resilience, rather than only building a list of everything wrong with their situation. For example, instead of just recording that a parent is struggling financially, you'd also note that they've kept their children in school every day despite that, and build the plan around that strength. I think it matters because people engage more honestly when they feel seen as capable, not just as a case file of problems, though I'd be careful it's never used as an excuse to withhold real support they need.

commonMistakes: Describing it as simply being positive or complimentary
Giving no concrete example of how it changes practice
Missing the risk of it masking genuine unmet need
followUps: Can you think of a situation where a strengths-based approach might not be enough on its own?

subtopic: Empowerment versus doing things for people
question: What's the difference between empowering a client and simply doing things for them?
lookingFor: Understanding that good social work builds people's own capacity and choices rather than creating dependency, while recognising some situations need direct action.

bullets: Define empowerment as helping someone build capacity and make their own choices
Contrast it with doing everything for a client, which can create dependency
Acknowledge some situations genuinely require the worker to act directly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Doing things for someone might solve the immediate problem, but it can leave them no better equipped for the next one, whereas empowering someone means helping them build the skills or confidence to handle it themselves, like sitting with someone while they make a difficult phone call instead of making it for them. That said, I don't think empowerment means stepping back in every situation, if someone is in crisis or at risk, direct action is sometimes exactly what's needed. It's about judging when someone needs support to act for themselves and when they need you to act for them.

commonMistakes: Treating empowerment as never intervening directly, even in crisis
Confusing empowerment with simply telling someone what to do
No example of what empowerment actually looks like day to day
followUps: How would you handle a client who wants you to just do it for them?

question: What does social justice mean to you in the context of social work practice?
lookingFor: Understanding that social work operates on both individual and structural levels, addressing unfair systems as well as individual need.

bullets: Distinguish helping an individual from addressing the structural cause of their problem
Give an example of advocacy at a systemic or policy level
Show awareness this can create tension with an employer or system
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: To me it means noticing when an individual's problem is really a symptom of something structural, like a family struggling not because of anything they've done but because of how a benefits system is designed, and being willing to push on that bigger picture, not just patch the individual case. That might mean writing to a local council about a housing policy, or supporting a group of service users to advocate for themselves collectively. I know that kind of advocacy can put a worker at odds with their own agency sometimes, and I think part of the skill is doing it constructively rather than just being oppositional.

commonMistakes: Reducing social justice to just being fair to individual clients
No example of advocacy beyond the individual case level
Not acknowledging any tension this can create with employers or systems
followUps: Can you think of a social policy issue you feel strongly about?

question: What do you understand by looking at a person 'in their environment', and why is that a core idea in social work?
lookingFor: Understanding that a person's behaviour and circumstances can't be fully understood without their family, community, and wider social context.

bullets: Explain that behaviour and struggles make more sense in the context of family, community, and systems around a person
Contrast this with an approach that only looks at the individual in isolation
Give a concrete example of how it changes an assessment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It means you can't really understand why someone is struggling by looking at just them in isolation, you have to look at their family, their neighbourhood, their school or workplace, and the systems they're dealing with, because all of that shapes what's actually happening. For example, a child acting out at school might look like a discipline problem on the surface, but if you look at their environment and find overcrowded housing and a parent working three jobs, the picture changes completely. That's why I think social work assessments have to be broader than just the individual, otherwise you risk blaming someone for a situation that's really about the system around them.

commonMistakes: Only describing the individual's behaviour with no mention of context
Confusing this with just gathering background information for its own sake
No concrete example connecting theory to practice
followUps: How might a social worker gather information about someone's environment in practice?

question: Social work is sometimes described as operating at micro, mezzo, and macro levels. What does that mean, and which level interests you most?
lookingFor: Accurate understanding of the three levels of practice, and a genuine, thought-out preference rather than a rehearsed answer.

bullets: Define micro as direct work with individuals or families
Define mezzo as work with groups or communities, and macro as policy or systems-level work
State a genuine preference with reasoning, while showing appreciation for the others
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Micro level is direct work with an individual or a family, mezzo is working with groups or communities, like running a support group or working with a school, and macro is the bigger systems and policy level, like campaigning for a change in legislation. I'm most drawn to micro practice at the moment, because I like the relationship-building and seeing change happen with a specific person, but I know that direct work only goes so far if the policy above it is broken, so I'd want to stay aware of the macro level even while working closely at the micro one.

commonMistakes: Confusing which level is which
Claiming to care equally about all three with no genuine preference
Describing macro-level work as unrelated to direct practice
followUps: How do decisions at the macro level end up affecting your work at the micro level?

question: What's the difference between empathy and sympathy, and why does that distinction matter for a social worker?
lookingFor: A clear understanding that empathy means genuinely trying to understand someone's experience, while sympathy can be more distant or pitying, and that only the former supports effective practice.

bullets: Define sympathy as feeling sorry for someone from the outside
Define empathy as trying to genuinely understand their experience from their perspective
Explain why empathy, not pity, is what supports a working relationship
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone, it keeps you a bit at a distance, looking at their situation from the outside and feeling bad about it. Empathy is trying to actually understand what it feels like from where they're standing, without necessarily having lived it yourself. I think that distinction matters a lot in social work because pity can come across as condescending and can shut someone down, whereas empathy is what actually builds enough trust for someone to be honest with you about what's really going on.

commonMistakes: Using the two words interchangeably with no real distinction
Describing empathy as just being nice
Not connecting it back to why it matters for building trust with a client
followUps: Can too much empathy ever get in the way of good practice?

question: Social work can be emotionally demanding. How do you plan to look after your own wellbeing while doing this kind of work?
lookingFor: Realistic self-awareness about the emotional toll of the profession and specific, credible strategies rather than a vague reassurance.

bullets: Show honest awareness that the work can be draining, not just rewarding
Name specific, realistic strategies, like supervision, peer support, or personal boundaries
Reference this as something to actively build as a skill, not assume will happen naturally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've seen from volunteering that even secondhand exposure to people's hardest moments takes something out of you, so I don't think I can just power through it on willpower. I plan to use supervision properly, actually raising difficult cases rather than just reporting facts, and I want to build a habit of debriefing with colleagues rather than carrying things home silently. I also think setting a real boundary between work and home, even something as simple as a proper commute routine, is something I need to build deliberately rather than assume will happen on its own.

commonMistakes: Claiming they're naturally resilient and won't struggle with it
Giving only vague answers like 'I'll take breaks'
Not acknowledging supervision or peer support as a real tool
followUps: What would you do if you noticed yourself becoming emotionally numb to clients' situations?

question: How would you handle working with a client whose lifestyle or choices strongly conflict with your own personal values?
lookingFor: Honest acknowledgement that bias exists, combined with a genuine strategy for managing it professionally rather than pretending to be unaffected.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly that personal reactions are normal, not something to deny
Explain how they'd separate personal judgement from professional duty
Mention using supervision or reflection to process the reaction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think it's realistic to say I'd feel nothing, everyone has values, but the job is to make sure my personal reaction doesn't shape how I treat the person or the quality of support they get. I'd try to notice the reaction when it happens rather than pretend it isn't there, and use supervision to talk it through honestly instead of letting it quietly affect my practice. What I'm there to do is understand their situation and meet their needs, not approve of their choices, and I think being upfront with myself about any bias is actually what makes it possible to set it aside.

commonMistakes: Claiming they would feel completely neutral about anything
Admitting bias but offering no strategy to manage it
Suggesting they'd hand the case to someone else rather than reflect on their own reaction
followUps: Can you think of an example from your own life where you had to set aside a judgement like that?

question: A client you've worked with for months offers you a gift as thanks. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: Understanding of why professional boundaries matter, handled with tact rather than a rigid, cold refusal.

bullets: Recognise the gesture as genuine and handle it with warmth, not suspicion
Explain the reasoning behind boundaries around gifts, like fairness and avoiding dual relationships
Describe a tactful way to decline or redirect it, following agency policy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to accept the kindness behind it without accepting the gift itself, so I'd thank them warmly and explain that I'm not able to accept gifts, not because I don't value what they're offering, but because it's a rule that applies to every client I work with so nobody gets treated differently. I'd check my agency's actual policy rather than just guessing, since some have specific thresholds or exceptions for small tokens. I'd also want to make sure declining it doesn't feel like a rejection of them personally, so I'd probably suggest another way to acknowledge the moment, like simply telling them how much the progress means to me too.

commonMistakes: Accepting the gift without thinking about the professional implications
Refusing bluntly in a way that could feel hurtful to the client
Not knowing that agencies typically have specific policies on this
followUps: Would your answer change if the gift were something small, like homemade food?

question: How would you try to build trust with a client who doesn't want you involved in their life?
lookingFor: Understanding that resistance is often reasonable rather than defiance, and a practical, patient approach to engagement.

bullets: Recognise resistance as often a rational response, not stubbornness
Describe being honest and transparent about the worker's role and limits
Show patience, building trust gradually rather than expecting instant cooperation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by assuming their reluctance makes sense, maybe they've had a bad experience with services before, or they feel judged, so I wouldn't take it personally or push too hard early on. I'd try to be really clear and honest about why I'm involved and what my role actually is, rather than letting them imagine the worst version of it. Mostly I think trust gets built slowly through consistency, showing up, following through on small things I've said I'd do, rather than through any one conversation, so I'd try not to expect a breakthrough too quickly.

commonMistakes: Treating resistance as simple defiance to be overcome
Suggesting they'd force engagement rather than build it gradually
No mention of being transparent about the worker's role
followUps: What would you do if that trust never fully developed?

question: How would you approach working with a family from a cultural background very different from your own?
lookingFor: Humility and a willingness to learn from the client rather than assuming expertise, plus awareness of the risk of imposing one's own norms.

bullets: Show humility, treating the family as the expert on their own culture and situation
Mention actively seeking to understand rather than assuming or generalising
Acknowledge the risk of unintentionally imposing your own cultural norms as 'correct'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd try to go in without assuming I already understand their situation just because I've read about their background in general, and instead ask them directly what matters to them and let them guide me on what's relevant. I think the risk is assuming my own norms around things like family structure or parenting are simply the neutral, correct ones, when they're just as culturally specific as anyone else's. I'd want to stay curious rather than performative about it, actually asking questions instead of just nodding along like I already know the answer.

commonMistakes: Claiming to already understand other cultures well from general reading
Treating cultural awareness as a checklist rather than an ongoing practice
Not acknowledging the risk of imposing their own cultural assumptions
followUps: What would you do if a cultural practice in the family conflicted with a child's safety?

question: What social issue in the news at the moment do you find yourself thinking about, and why does it matter to social work?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with current affairs relevant to the profession, with a considered rather than superficial take.

bullets: Name a specific, real, current issue rather than something vague
Explain the connection to social work practice specifically
Show a considered, balanced view rather than just an opinion
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following the coverage of the shortage of children's social workers and the caseloads that leaves people carrying, because it's not just a staffing story, it directly affects how much attention any one family actually gets and how much risk can slip through. It's made me think about the tension between wanting to do this work and walking into a system that's already stretched, and I've tried to read up on what's actually being proposed to fix it rather than just feeling discouraged by the headlines. I think it matters to me because it's the practical reality I'd be stepping into, not an abstract policy debate.

commonMistakes: Naming an issue with no real connection to social work
Giving only a surface-level opinion with no depth
Sounding like they haven't actually followed the story beyond a headline
followUps: What do you think could realistically be done about it?

question: Social workers often work alongside teachers, nurses, and police. Why is this kind of multidisciplinary working important, and what challenges might it bring?
lookingFor: Understanding of why interagency work matters for a full picture of a person's situation, plus realistic awareness of coordination challenges.

bullets: Explain that each profession sees a different piece of a person's situation
Give a concrete reason coordinated information sharing improves outcomes
Acknowledge realistic challenges like differing priorities or poor communication
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Every profession only sees one slice of someone's life, a teacher sees a child at school, a nurse sees them at a health visit, and no single person has the full picture on their own, so working together is often the only way anyone catches a pattern that matters. I've read about cases where things went wrong partly because information that different professionals held separately was never actually put together. The challenge is that everyone has different priorities and sometimes different language for the same concern, so I think part of the skill is being the person who can translate between those perspectives rather than assuming everyone already agrees.

commonMistakes: Describing it as simply 'working as a team' with no specific reasoning
Ignoring the real coordination and communication challenges involved
Assuming all professions naturally share the same priorities
followUps: What would you do if another professional disagreed with your assessment of a case?

question: How do you think poverty affects the kinds of situations a social worker deals with?
lookingFor: Understanding that poverty is often an underlying driver of the presenting problem, not a side detail, without reducing every case to poverty alone.

bullets: Explain how financial hardship can drive or worsen the problem a family presents with
Avoid treating poverty as the explanation for everything, or as a moral failing
Show awareness that addressing poverty is often partly structural, not just individual
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of what looks like a parenting problem or a family conflict on the surface often has money stress running underneath it, someone working long hours across multiple jobs has less time and less patience, and that shows up in a household in ways that get misread as the real issue. I don't think poverty explains every situation a social worker sees, and I'd be careful not to assume it does, but I do think it's often part of the picture that needs naming rather than ignoring. It's also not something an individual worker can fix alone, which is why I think social work has to sit alongside pushing for better structural support, not just individual casework.

commonMistakes: Treating poverty as a personal failing of the family
Reducing every case to poverty with no nuance
Assuming an individual worker can single-handedly solve structural poverty
followUps: What role, if any, do you think a social worker has in addressing poverty beyond the individual case?

question: Tell us about a time you supported someone going through a difficult situation. What did you do, and what did you learn?
lookingFor: A specific, honest story demonstrating patience and real listening, with genuine reflection.

bullets: Describe a real, specific situation, not a generic one
Focus on what they actually did, especially listening rather than fixing
End with a genuine reflection on what it taught them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My neighbour's teenage son ran away from home for a few days last year, and she was frantic, so I spent most evenings that week just sitting with her while she waited for news, not really saying much useful, just being there. What I learned was that I kept wanting to reassure her that it would be fine, and I had to stop myself, because she didn't actually want false comfort, she wanted someone to sit in the uncertainty with her honestly. When he came home safe, she told me the sitting there mattered more than anything I'd said, and that's stuck with me since.

commonMistakes: Choosing a story where they mainly talk about giving advice, not listening
Vague or generic story with no real specific detail
No genuine reflection on what was learned
followUps: How did you know when to just listen versus when to say something?

question: A client asks whether you've been through something similar to what they're facing. Would you tell them?
lookingFor: Thoughtful judgement about self-disclosure, weighing potential connection against professional focus, rather than a blanket yes or no.

bullets: Recognise self-disclosure can build connection but isn't automatically a good idea
Explain they'd consider whose need it serves, the client's or their own
Show they'd keep any disclosure brief and refocus back on the client
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't have a fixed rule against it, because a small, honest disclosure can sometimes make a client feel less alone, but I'd think carefully about whose need it's really serving before I said anything. If I answered, I'd try to keep it brief and steer the conversation straight back to them, because the session is about their situation, not mine, and I wouldn't want to accidentally shift the focus onto my own story. I think the test I'd use is whether sharing it genuinely helps them open up, versus whether it's really just me wanting to be understood too.

commonMistakes: Saying they would never share anything personal under any circumstance
Saying they'd freely share personal details without considering the impact
Not distinguishing between disclosure that serves the client and disclosure that serves the worker
followUps: What would make you decide not to disclose in a given moment?

question: How would you cope with hearing about a genuinely distressing situation, like abuse or neglect, and still function professionally straight afterward?
lookingFor: Realistic, specific coping strategies and awareness that professional composure in the moment doesn't mean suppressing the impact permanently.

bullets: Distinguish staying composed in the moment from processing it properly afterward
Name a specific, realistic strategy for the immediate moment, like grounding or a brief pause
Mention deliberately processing it later, through supervision or debrief, rather than pushing it down
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In the moment I think staying steady is about focusing on the person in front of me and what they need right then, not on my own reaction, so I'd try to keep my attention outward rather than let the shock take over. But I don't think staying composed means pretending it didn't affect me, so afterward I'd want to actually process it, whether that's a proper debrief with a colleague or raising it in supervision, rather than just moving straight to the next task and burying it. I'd rather build the habit of dealing with it honestly early on than find it building up unnoticed over months.

commonMistakes: Claiming they simply wouldn't be affected by distressing content
Describing only suppressing the reaction with no plan to process it later
Giving a vague answer with no specific coping strategy
followUps: What would you do if you noticed a colleague struggling to cope after a difficult case?
